explanations.answer: Whether God will forget him forever
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David, Israel's king, asks, "Will You forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). He doesn't dress it up first. I think it took real nerve to say that straight to the LORD.

explanations.answer: Whether God will send rain soon
explanations.explanation: Rain would be a fine thing to ask about, friend, but David never brings up the weather. After "How long, O LORD?" he asks, "Will You forget me forever?" That question is about being remembered, not about the forecast. David, Israel's king, has his mind on something much closer than a cloud.

explanations.answer: Whether God will make him rich
explanations.explanation: I'd love a bigger bakery myself, baker, but money never comes up in this psalm. David, Israel's king, asks, "Will You forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). He wants the LORD's attention, not a fatter wallet. Nothing in his question has a price tag on it.

His enemy, baker. David, Israel's king, asks, "How long will my enemy dominate me?" (Psalm 13:2). The psalm never says who this enemy is. The enemy shows up again in verse 4, so I think he's weighing on David's mind.

A brother would be a whole season of family drama, friend, but this psalm doesn't go there. David, Israel's king, says it's his enemy who dominates him (Psalm 13:2). The psalm doesn't name that enemy, so I won't make up a name either. Brothers will have to wait for another passage.

A servant doing the dominating would be a wild twist, like the dough bossing the baker around. But David, Israel's king, never mentions a servant here. He asks, "How long will my enemy dominate me?" (Psalm 13:2). The enemy is the one on his mind.

True, baker. David asks the LORD, "Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death," (Psalm 13:3). Notice he's asking, not demanding. He calls Him "O LORD my God" right before it, and I think that says a lot about who he's turning to.

This one is actually true, friend. The text says, "Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death," (Psalm 13:3). David says it right to the LORD, who he calls "my God." Easy to doubt a line this heavy, but he really did say it.
Not quite, baker. David doesn't say his foes will mourn. He says, "…and my foes rejoice when I fall." (Psalm 13:4). Nobody is sad in that picture except David. I think that's the part that stings.

False is the answer, friend. Instead of mourning, David says, "…and my foes rejoice when I fall." (Psalm 13:4). A foe who sends flowers would be a nice change, but that's not this psalm. Their cheering is exactly what David doesn't want.

That's it, baker. David says, "But I have trusted in Your loving devotion;" (Psalm 13:5). He asked all those hard questions, and then he said where his trust is. It's a short turn, but it changes the whole psalm.

David was a warrior, so I get the guess, friend. But he never mentions a weapon in this psalm. He says, "But I have trusted in Your loving devotion;" (Psalm 13:5). Even with enemies around, his trust goes to the LORD, not to his gear.

A crew of mighty men sounds like good backup, baker, and I'd want them in my bakery if the ovens ever got rowdy. But this psalm never brings them up. David says, "But I have trusted in Your loving devotion;" (Psalm 13:5). His trust is in the LORD's devotion.
Heart is right, friend. David says, "my heart will rejoice in Your salvation." (Psalm 13:5). Back in verse 2 he had sorrow in his heart each day. Now that same heart is the one that will rejoice.

A rejoicing house would be quite the sight, baker, with the walls doing a little dance. But David says, "my heart will rejoice in Your salvation." (Psalm 13:5). The rejoicing starts on the inside, in his heart. Houses can stay quiet.
An army rejoicing would make a lot of noise, friend. But the psalm never mentions one. David says, "my heart will rejoice in Your salvation." (Psalm 13:5). The one rejoicing is his own heart.

explanations.answer: The LORD has been good to him
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David says, "I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me." (Psalm 13:6). His reason is the LORD's goodness. I think that's worth remembering the next time a hard day tries to talk loud.

explanations.answer: His enemy has finally run off
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, friend, but the psalm never says the enemy left. David's reason is, "I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me." (Psalm 13:6). He sings because of who the LORD is and what He has done. The enemy never even makes the reason list.

I can see why you'd guess that, baker, but the psalm doesn't say his sorrow lifted. David gives this reason: "I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me." (Psalm 13:6). His song rests on the LORD's goodness, not on how he feels that day. Hmm, that's a pretty good trick if you can do it.
